newsitem.title: GERMANY: Higher German CPI not seen as rate rise trigger.
newsitem.headline: Higher German CPI not seen as rate rise trigger.

text.p: Three German states reported higher cost of living in July on Wednesday, but economists insisted the pickup in price pressures would not force the Bundesbank to raise key interest rates in the near-term.

While economists differed over the reasons for the rise in the state inflation data, they agreed there was little reason for the wary Bundesbank to tighten monetary policy yet. Views were divided as to weather the mark's weakness on foreign exchange markets had fanned inflation pressures.

"There is no need to panic," said Holger Fahrinkrug, senior Germany economist at UBS in Frankfurt. "The Bundesbank will do nothing for some time to come." The central bank's policy-making council next meets on Thursday.

The states of Hesse, Bavaria and North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany's most populated states, all showed prices ticking higher in July compared with levels in Jube. The statistics office noted that higher costs in the services sector, along with health and beauty products, were behind the trend. Food prices were mostly lower.

Germany's statistics office uses data from the nation's four largest states to compile the preliminary west German inflation rate, which is expected to be released for July this week. The fourth state, Baden-Wuerttemberg, is also due to release price data in the next few days.
Fahrinkrug said the reason for July's higher inflation data was solely due to an increase in the portion of money Germans must pay toward medications, reflected in the rise of health care products.

The impact of the weaker mark on the data, however, remains disputed among economists. While the softer mark benefits German exporters by making their goods cheaper abroad, it also makes foreign goods more expensive for Germans.
Economists have been warning for some time that the mark's level, which is currently trading at 71-month lows of around 1.8325 marks to the dollar, would soon fan German inflation.

Armin Kayser, economist at SBC Warburg in Frankfurt said: "Slowly the effects of the softer mark are filtering into the cost of living prices," adding this move had been expected in light of the mark's sharp drop since the beginning of the year.

But Fahrinkrug said currency levels had not impacted the data. "The mark's levels have nothing to do with the inflation data," Fahrinkrug said, noting food prices, some of which were surely imported, were in fact quite moderate in July.
While the Bundesbank is sure to scrutinize these numbers, economists believe that inflationary pressures were nowhere near levels which would set off any sort of alarm bells at the central bank.
In light of Germany's fragile economic recovery, economists agreed the Bundesbank would do much more harm than good by raising interest rates at this point.
"The Bundesbank will not do anything for some time, as it would hurt the economy by raising rates prematurely," Fahrinkrug said.

Wednesday's data showed that prices in Hesse climbed 0.5 percent month-on-month and 1.6 percent year-on-year in July, after rising 0.3 percent and 1.5 percent respectively in June. In Bavaria prices increased 0.5 percent on the month and 1.7 percent on the year, also up on June levels
The statistics office in North Rhine-Westphalia said prices climbed 0.5 percent on the month and 2.1 percent on the year after rising 0.2 percent on the month and 1.9 percent on the year in June.
